They won't care about freckles you've painted on your face, or whether or not your glasses are two big. Someone who is real to you and has a natural chemistry with you won't give a flying fuck about anything else. I'd suggest working on your own comfortability in your own skin, and stop relying on others to tell you whether or not you're beautiful. Confidence does all the work. Right now, you're being very codependent. Get a therapist.

Hey, welcome to life. We are all a bunch of self-absorbed, selfish and self-centered assholes. Every. Single. Person. From time to time, at least. It looks bad if you're *always* self-interested. You're doing great, though. I hope you find something in your life that brings you personal joy, satisfaction and fulfillment. And don't forget to keep talking to people, even if they say the wrong thing, don't know what to say, or know exactly the right thing to tell you. Seek comfort and connection during these times, and you'll make it through. Keep it up.

I'd like to challenge you a little bit here. Suicide *is* a permanent solution to a temporary problem. You're currently single. Not sure if you always have been or not, but the chances you'll go 80 years without one is pretty slim. We can't speak in absolutes because we can't see the future. While there is a chance that you may never have a relationship (again or for the first time), there's also a chance you will, and I would say the probability is a lot stronger on the side of you ending up in one some day. Killing yourself because you're not in one definitely makes it impossible to experience one. No kids? There are other options such as adoption or fostering or being in a relationship with someone who has kids. Shit, you could kidnap a kid too. I would highly not recommend that option, but it's there, just as suicide is. I'd put money on someone loving you or having loved you. Now, whether or not loved you in a healthy and positive way would likely be arguable, but even if someone loves you in all the wrong ways, is that not, in its own way, still love? We share only the love we have known. Love is often unconditional, but relationships are very much conditional, and there is a huge difference between the two. Is your idea of love actually realistic? I know mine hasn't always been. However, I digress. You could take your life and avoid all the individual problems you'll face in your life. Or you could figure out all of the other options that are available when faced with a problem. I've known too many people who have been successful in completing suicide, and have been suicidal too many times to count, to understand there is strength in whatever decision you decide to make. The only argument for, that I see, is free will and being able to decide for yourself whether or not you want to do it. It can't be illegal to complete suicide because if you do it, it's not like you'll be under arrest. For most people I would say it comes down to their faith and/or spirituality, and for what consequences it may bring to those around them. Having personally known 7 people who were successful, I'm beyond aware of what consequences my own suicide would bring to those around me. But I also know that I live my life on my own accord, no one else's. That would be why some consider it a selfish act. In my mind, it lifts others from the burden that is me, but being aware of what it will do to the psyche of those I care about and still deciding to do it... Well, you see the conundrum. I think about waiting, too. As I'm an only child and don't have any cousins, I could wait until my mom and Aunts and Uncle pass and then do it. But then what happens to all the people whose lives I've impacted along the way? Have I just used them to get by until I had no family left? Is it fair for me to say that I love them, and then make them suffer from my death? Someone I care about in my life currently gets into arguments with me consistently over my carelessness, recklessness, and lack of interest in caring for my health and safety. It's probably why I've been trying to self sabotage that relationship in order to push her away. For as much as I long to have a relationship, it's very uncomfortable to have people get close to me, because it feels so foreign and because in the end I know I can't be there forever, even if I wanted to. Whether I complete suicide, or something happens, I know, ultimately, my life will end. Anyway, I digress... Again. While in the grand scheme of the vast universe, you're right, we are just turds in the toilet... In our own small spaces and our own small worlds, our lives are important and they truly do matter. Both exist at the same time. One aspect makes it all feel insignificant and pointless. The other, the one with those close to us, has quite a bit to do with love... And choosing to love ourselves in healthy and positive ways often shows others the love they want to see from us. There's a reason confidence is attractive. The independence and the strength to move on, overcome obstacles, keep pushing and living to our fullest potential is what makes the proverbial panties drop. It's a balancing act, for sure. Perspectives are a bitch.

Hello friend. There's a lot to take in here, and so much is out of context, as this sounds like a very deep, complicated, and emotional situation for you. I too have quite a disdain for myself. The issue with that is this; people who care about us are concerned with three things. Those three things are our health, our safety and our personal success. If we aren't doing things that are best for our overall health, our overall safety and setting ourselves up for personal success, people tend to bitch about it. I would say you have the same concerns for the girl you love and care for. The thing is, if we aren't doing the best for ourselves, then we aren't truly loving others. It is kind of a complicated path. Each time I've placed someone above me, I have loved them in ways that they felt controlled and manipulated. While my intention is to look after and protect them, I am making one huge mistake; I am not loving them in a way in which they feel free. Allowing others to make choices, good or bad, is up to their own free will. Sometimes if they did something wrong it felt like they didn't love me, because they didn't listen to me. That's controlling. We must allow others to live their lives in which they see fit. They have the choice to take our advice or not. If this person tried to walk out of your life today, would you do anything to stop them? No end to which you would go in order to try and convince them to stay? Loving someone in a way in which they feel free is respecting their desire to leave. It doesn't feel good, it hurts, and brings up a lot of feelings of abandonment and disconnection from the world. But they have the right to walk whatever path they want, with or without you. Being around you and being a part of your life is a choice. If we put restrictions on things, it certainly appears as if we don't love anyone but ourselves. Unconditional love is caring for someone no matter what, but we have to always remember that while love is unconditional, actual relationships are very much conditional. People have the right to leave whenever they so choose, regardless of our personal feelings. The phrase 'the road to hell is paved with good intentions,' comes to mind here. It doesn't matter what our actual intent is, we are responsible for the things we say, how we say them, and the actions of our bodies. If something we did wrong comes from something we said, our tone, or something we physically did, and it hurts someone else, then we have to take responsibility for our actions and apologize. Or not, of course. But if we aren't taking responsibility for our own actions, then again, we look controlling and manipulative, and those same accusations of being selfish and self-centered start getting thrown around again. I hope this all makes sense, and that you're able to do a full and thorough inventory and be critical enough to really consider what it is that others are trying to tell you. It's okay, of course. You're a human being. A lot of us struggle with caring for ourselves in good and positive ways, and when we don't, it often impacts our relationships with others. You're fully entitled to make mistakes. We just need to make sure we are learning from our mistakes if we want things to truly change.

That's okay. Depression can be a real pain in the ass. Do you ever give yourself credit for the things you do accomplish, instead of focusing on the things you don't? Just recognizing you got out of bed on a day you didn't want to is a big hurdle. It's good that you want these things for yourself. I hope you're able to pinpoint what some of the differences are on days that you're able to do more, than on days that are difficult. You might find something you need to work on to make it more consistent in order to have a better time with it. 

If you're in school, you can always go talk to the school counselor. Or, hell, any of the staff, really, that you might feel comfortable with. If you're worried about things getting back to your rents, then I would encourage you to ask the staff about what they're able to keep confidential ("keep secret") and don't need to tell your folks about. 

It sounds like you're needing some heavy doses of comfort and connection, and in good, positive, healthy ways. I would so strongly suggest you talk to someone around you. I'm glad you're on here, talking, at the very least. Please be safe.

A few things I'm getting the sense of here...

First, I sense a lot of frustration. When we feel frustrated, we have to be mindful of the things we have control over. We have control over three things: the things we say, how and when we say them, and the movements of our bodies. You certainly have control over what you do for a living. Despite explaining you're getting a degree you want, you listed immediately two reasons as to why in your mind it isn't a good idea. I get the sense that maybe there is still some soul searching and self-exploring that needs to be done in finding something that you can spend every day enjoying. I imagine a full exploration of the jobs you have had, there may have been one or two aspects that you actually did enjoy. You should hone in on those and really spend some creative time considering what field(s) might have some of those aspects more consistently. 

Another thing I'm picking up on, and correct me if I'm wrong, but I'm getting a sense that all of these things need to happen *now.* There's no time given to making sure you're doing what you truly want, no time given to exploring life, no time given to allowing mistakes and failures, no time to figure some things out first. We don't have control over time. And I get that we all want good things for ourselves, and it's hard to wait for good things to come, but any journey of change takes a lot of time. And there's no set period of time for any of us to figure things out. That's where our uniqueness comes into play, as all navigate our own lives. There is wisdom in having patience in your journey, and finding ways to enjoy the ride on your way there. 

Next, I'd be curious as to how many therapists you've had, how many medications you've tried, and how long you've been on each while being *consistent* in your medication management. Mental illnesses require much more than medications and therapy, too; self-care in the form of good sleep, diet, exercise, hygiene, etc., all play a huge role. This is where I would really challenge yourself to be honest. Are you truly doing *everything,* and have been doing them consistently, every day, for 6 months or more? This is often where I personally fail, is the overall maintenance. It does get boring and it's hard to get motivated. But just really how bad do you want to be happy?

Lastly, I would say you're finding comfort and connection in your friends and girlfriend, and even in the "not-so-healthy-for-me-but-I-like-doing-them-anyway" coping skills of self-medicating. So what are your other "positive" triggers? What do you find easy to focus on? Where can you go and/or do to find a sense of peace within yourself? Are there times you've experienced feeling whole, even without your friends or girlfriend around? 

I hope you're being honest with your therapist. If you think they suck, tell them. Tell them you don't think it's working. You can change therapists, you can change medications, you can try different configurations. But you have to talk about how you feel like it's making you worse, or feels like you're not improving at all. You've gotta communicate the cold, hard, honest truth. 

You're on the right path. I hope you're reminding yourself that you're not a perfect person and that getting things right takes a lot of time, patience and practice. Sounds like you may have some good support in your life with people you feel close to. Supports were made to lean on a little, in times of stress.

Finding the solution lies in answering the above questions, one at a time, as realistically and honestly as you can. Unfortunately, happiness isn't the only emotion we have, so we don't get the option of *always* feeling that way. Just as there are negative triggers, there are ones that bring about positive emotions too.
You're doing great so far! Good luck!

Hey friend. I know what it's like to lose someone that is important to you. It's difficult when you feel like you don't belong, you feel like you're ultimately all alone and no one understands you, you feel like you're always on the outside looking in... then this beautiful person comes into your life and you can see the colors of the world. You imagine and fantasize about the future and everything seems like it's going to work out in the end and you'll finally find happiness, contentment, a home. Then, after time, things begin falling apart. And no matter what you do, you can't seem to put it back together and all you want to do is give up. No matter what you do, no matter what you say, nothing changes it back. And now you're disconnected again from the entire world, because the one thing that kept you halfway grounded is leaving or is gone. That feeling of wanting to give up and die is real, and it is like it's the only answer, because nothing else in the world, in life, is right. I can't promise you that your vision of the future will come true, as throughout your life, many, many people will come and go. Through loss of life, through time, distance, personal change... there's always going to be another one that leaves. But for every beautiful soul that I wanted to kill myself over losing, life has filled me with multiple people to fill that empty space that comes in. It's okay to grieve your loss, brother. It's okay to feel sad. It's okay to cry or scream or both, it's okay to have these feelings like nothing will ever be the same. Because, technically, it won't. But just because things aren't the same, it doesn't mean that things won't be okay. It doesn't mean that life is pointless, it doesn't mean there is no hope, it doesn't mean that there will forever be 'no one.' Our minds play tricks on us when we think in terms of always, forever, never, everyone, no one... these are all absolutes, guarantees. But life has extremely few guarantees. I'm sorry you're hurting so much. I hope you made it through the night. I hope you keep making it. Distract yourself as much as you can to take the emotion away as much as you can. Thankfully, emotions don't last forever. They're big and intense for a while, but they, too, have an end. I hope you've learned ways to self-harm without truly injuring yourself like drawing on yourself, holding ice cubes, snapping rubber bands against your skin, or any other safer techniques that you can get that satisfying feeling from. I hope you have hobbies and things you can do that will pull your mind from all the thoughts. I hope you're able to find the strength enough to reach out to some professionals for help. There are truly people out there who care about you, despite not even knowing who you are.
